questions.prompt: A conditional returns Counter in the same tree position in both branches. What preserves its state?

choices.text: The same text appears in the returned JSX regardless of type.
The branches have different source-code line numbers.
The same component type remains at the same tree position.
The component has exactly the same primitive prop values.

questions.explanation: React tracks the resulting tree position rather than source-code branch placement. Changed props alone need not reset state.

sources.title: Preserving and Resetting State
sources.claim: React associates state with component position and type in the render tree; stable sibling keys identify components, while changing type or key can reset state and keys are local to their parent.

questions.prompt: Two Counter instances appear at different tree positions. How is their local state stored?

choices.text: Independently only when their props contain unique IDs.
Independently, because each occupies a distinct tree position.
Together, because hook calls share one module-level object.
Together, because both call the same Counter function.

questions.explanation: Distinct positions have distinct component state even with the same function and props.

questions.prompt: A div wrapper changes to section at the same position around a Counter. What can happen to Counter state?

choices.text: It is preserved whenever Counter function code has not changed.
It is copied automatically from the removed wrapper subtree.
It is preserved because the text inside the Counter is unchanged.
It resets because React replaces the differently typed subtree.

questions.explanation: Changing the host type causes the old subtree to be removed; its descendant state is not carried to the new subtree.

questions.prompt: Why can defining a component function inside its parent reset child state across parent renders?

choices.text: React identifies the child by its function name rather than identity.
A new function identity is treated as a different component type.
Every nested function shares the same state storage as its parent.
Nested functions guarantee that the old state follows their name.

questions.explanation: A newly created function is a new component type. Declare component functions at stable top-level positions.

questions.prompt: An editable list is reordered. Which key best keeps each draft with its record?

choices.text: A fresh random number generated during every render.
The stable database ID belonging to that record.
The shared list title used by every sibling element.
The current array index after the new sort is applied.

questions.explanation: Stable record IDs preserve identity across reordering. Position-based or changing keys can move or reset state.

questions.prompt: A chat form should discard its draft when recipient changes. Which change intentionally resets it?

choices.text: Move draft text into a module variable shared by all recipients.
Change a label prop while keeping its component identity unchanged.
Set the form key to the selected recipient stable ID.
Read the recipient name from the same existing closure.

questions.explanation: Changing the key creates a different identity at that position and resets its local state.

questions.prompt: Which statements about tree-position identity are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Identical prop values make instances at different tree positions share state.
A preserved position and type can retain state across changed props.
Moving a component always transfers its state to any new location.
Every call of one component function shares the same state.
Two instances of one component can have separate local state.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: state belongs to each component identity, even with identical props. B: Correct: props can update without replacing identity. C: Incorrect: a different position can create a different identity. D: Incorrect: the function is not one global state slot. E: Correct: distinct positions are distinct instances.

questions.prompt: Which changes can reset an existing subtree state? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Change only a text prop while preserving type and key.
Replace the component at a position with a different type.
Create a new nested component function on each parent render.
Reuse the same stable type and sibling key in the same parent.
Remove the subtree and later create it again.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: changed props alone do not replace identity. B: Correct: different types replace stateful identity. C: Correct: a new function identity can replace the type. D: Incorrect: this normally preserves identity. E: Correct: removed component state is discarded.

questions.prompt: Which key choices support reliable sibling identity? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Generate new keys on each render to preserve old drafts.
Keep keys unique among siblings under the same parent.
Avoid index identity when records can be reordered.
Use a stable ID associated with each list record.
Require each key to be globally unique across every app root.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: changing keys resets identities. B: Correct: sibling identity must be unambiguous. C: Correct: positions do not consistently identify reordered records. D: Correct: IDs follow their records. E: Incorrect: key uniqueness is scoped to the parent.

questions.prompt: Which behaviors follow from intentionally changing a form key? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A recipient ID key can keep one draft from carrying into another chat.
Only the element label changes while all local state must survive.

The old draft is copied automatically into the new form.
State inside the old keyed subtree is reset.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: the documented chat example uses this reset pattern. B: Incorrect: a key change can replace the subtree. C: Correct: different keys distinguish identities. D: Incorrect: the old local state is discarded. E: Correct: new identity starts fresh state.
